option_description: Controls whether any screen lock mechanism is active on the device. When enabled, the device requires a credential (PIN, password, pattern, or biometric) to unlock after idle timeout or manual lock. When false, the device screen can be dismissed without any authentication.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'weak_or_absent_device_screen_lock' exposure when 'not input.screen_lock_enabled' evaluates to true. A missing screen lock grants immediate physical access to all on-device application data, cached credentials, session tokens, and stored documents without any authentication barrier. This is a high-criticality, score-8 finding under physical_security.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android: navigate to Settings > Security > Screen Lock and observe whether a lock type other than None or Swipe is configured. On iOS: navigate to Settings > Face ID & Passcode (or Touch ID & Passcode) and confirm a passcode is set.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Android: Settings > Security > Screen Lock | iOS: Settings > Face ID & Passcode
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Android shows PIN, Pattern, Password, or Fingerprint as the active lock type. iOS shows passcode fields are enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM console for the device compliance profile. In Microsoft Intune, retrieve the device compliance state via Graph API and check the 'isCompliant' and 'passcodePresent' fields. For Jamf Pro, query /api/v1/mobile-devices/{id}/detail and inspect the 'mobileDeviceManagement.passcodePresent' attribute.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response JSON contains 'passcodePresent': true for a compliant device.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On an Android device with ADB access (for assessment purposes), query the device policy manager to determine whether a password quality policy is enforced by the device admin.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell dumpsys device_policy | grep -i 'password quality\|screen lock'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output includes 'mPasswordQuality' set to a value other than 0 (PASSWORD_QUALITY_UNSPECIFIED), confirming a lock policy is active.

option_description: Identifies the specific authentication mechanism protecting the device lock screen. Values range from 'none' (no lock) through progressively stronger options: 'swipe' (gesture with no credential), 'pin' (numeric-only), 'pattern' (graphical connect-the-dots), 'password' (alphanumeric), and 'biometric' (fingerprint or face recognition, which always requires a PIN/password fallback).
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'weak_or_absent_device_screen_lock' when 'input.screen_lock_type in ["none", "swipe"]'. Swipe provides zero security — it cannot resist any deliberate access attempt. 'pin' and 'pattern' are accepted only when combined with a max-attempts policy; without that constraint they are vulnerable to brute-force under the third Rego condition. This attribute directly determines the credential strength tier for the physical_security exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android: navigate to Settings > Security > Screen Lock and note the highlighted/selected lock type. On iOS: navigate to Settings > Face ID & Passcode and observe whether a numeric or alphanumeric passcode is configured (iOS does not label as 'pin' vs 'password' directly; choose 'Passcode Options' during setup to confirm type).
how_to_obtain.navigation: Android: Settings > Security > Screen Lock | iOS: Settings > Face ID & Passcode > Passcode Options
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Android screen shows the currently selected lock type highlighted. iOS shows the active passcode entry field style (6-digit numeric vs. custom alphanumeric).

how_to_obtain.instruction: In VMware Workspace ONE UEM, call the device details API and inspect the 'ComplianceStatus' block along with the 'PasscodeCompliant' and 'PasscodeCompliantWithProfiles' fields to infer lock type policy enforcement.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response includes 'PasscodeCompliant': true and MDM profile-enforced password quality settings indicating type.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Using ADB on Android, dump the device policy manager service output to read the enforced password quality constant, which maps to specific lock types.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell dumpsys device_policy | grep -A2 'Password quality'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Shows 'mPasswordQuality=196608' (PASSWORD_QUALITY_ALPHANUMERIC) or similar constant; 65536=NUMERIC (pin), 131072=NUMERIC_COMPLEX, 196608=ALPHABETIC, 262144=ALPHANUMERIC.

option_description: Controls whether the device enforces a hard limit on consecutive failed unlock attempts. When configured, the device wipes itself or enters escalating lockout after the threshold is reached. When false, an attacker with physical access can attempt unlimited passcode guesses without triggering any protective response.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'weak_or_absent_device_screen_lock' specifically when 'input.screen_lock_enabled == true', 'not input.screen_lock_max_attempts_configured', AND 'input.screen_lock_type in ["pin", "pattern"]'. This recognizes that PIN and pattern locks have limited keyspaces and become trivially brute-forceable without a lockout policy. Even a 6-digit PIN (1,000,000 combinations) is exhausted in under an hour at one attempt per second if no wipe threshold is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS: navigate to Settings > Face ID & Passcode (or Touch ID & Passcode) and scroll to locate 'Erase Data'. Confirm the toggle is enabled; this activates the 10-attempt wipe policy. On Android: navigate to Settings > Security > Screen Lock > (gear icon or settings) > Automatically wipe device or Automatically lock.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > Face ID & Passcode > Erase Data toggle | Android: Settings > Security > Screen Lock settings > Automatically wipe
how_to_obtain.expected_output: iOS shows 'Erase Data' toggle ON. Android shows a configured attempt limit (e.g., 10 attempts before wipe).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Microsoft Intune via Graph API for the device configuration profile and inspect the 'passwordMaximumAttemptCount' property within the device restriction profile applied to the device.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON returns policy objects with 'passwordMaximumAttemptCount' set to a non-null, non-zero integer (typically 6–10) confirming enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android via ADB, query the device policy manager for the configured maximum failed password attempts value set by the active device administrator.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell dumpsys device_policy | grep -i 'maximum failed'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows 'mMaximumFailedPasswordsForWipe=10' or similar non-zero value; zero or absent means no limit is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the MDM administrator to export the compliance policy report for enrolled devices and confirm that the 'maxFailedPasswordAttempts' or equivalent field is set and non-zero across the device fleet.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Exported CSV or PDF policy report shows all managed devices have a configured failed-attempt threshold of 10 or fewer.

option_description: Indicates whether full-disk encryption (FDE) or file-based encryption (FBE) is active on the device storage layer. On Android this is a configurable security setting controlling whether the userdata partition is encrypted at rest. On iOS, hardware encryption is automatically active when a passcode is set on supported hardware, making passcode presence the proxy indicator.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'unencrypted_device_storage' when 'not input.device_encryption_enabled'. Without encryption, raw device storage extracted via forensic tools (e.g., Cellebrite, UFED), JTAG probing, or chip-off techniques exposes the entire userdata partition in plaintext — including application databases, authentication tokens, cached API responses, and keychain entries accessible outside the secure enclave. This is a high-criticality, score-8 physical_security finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android: navigate to Settings > Security > Encryption & Credentials (path varies by OEM; may appear as Settings > Biometrics and Security > Encrypt Device on Samsung). Confirm status shows 'Encrypted'. On iOS: encryption is implicitly active when a passcode is set; verify via Settings > Face ID & Passcode confirming a passcode is enabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Android: Settings > Security > Encryption & Credentials | iOS: Settings > Face ID & Passcode
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Android displays 'Encrypted' status. iOS passcode is enabled, confirming hardware encryption is gated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android via ADB, query the vold (volume daemon) properties to confirm file-based encryption state.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell getprop ro.crypto.state && adb shell getprop ro.crypto.type
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ro.crypto.state' returns 'encrypted'; 'ro.crypto.type' returns 'file' (FBE on Android 7+) or 'block' (FDE on older devices).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Jamf Pro's MDM API for the mobile device detail record and inspect the 'storageEncryptionEnabled' or 'dataProtectionEnabled' fields in the security section.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response includes 'data_protection': true and 'block_level_encryption_capable': true with 'passcode_lock': true confirming encryption is active.

option_description: Captures the encryption compliance state as evaluated and reported by the enrolled Mobile Device Management system. Unlike the device-self-reported 'device_encryption_enabled' field, this reflects whether the MDM has successfully verified the encryption posture against the organization's defined compliance policy baseline. 'compliant' means the MDM has confirmed encryption is active and meeting policy; 'non_compliant' means encryption is absent or policy requirements are unmet; 'unknown' means the MDM has not assessed or cannot confirm the state.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'unencrypted_device_storage' independently when 'input.mdm_compliance_encryption_status == "non_compliant"', and fires again when the status is 'unknown' combined with 'not input.passcode_set'. The 'unknown' condition is critical: an MDM that cannot assess encryption state provides no assurance, and without a passcode the iOS hardware encryption gate is not engaged. 'non_compliant' is an unambiguous signal of unprotected storage warranting immediate remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, retrieve the managed device's compliance state via Microsoft Graph API, filtering for the encryption compliance policy result.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array contains a policy state entry with 'settingName': 'storageRequireEncryption' and 'state': 'compliant' or 'nonCompliant'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the MDM admin console (Intune, Jamf Pro, Workspace ONE), navigate to the device record and open the Compliance or Hardware/Security detail tab. Locate the Encryption Status or Data Protection field.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune: Devices > All Devices > [Device] > Device Compliance | Jamf Pro: Devices > [Device] > Security | Workspace ONE: Devices > [Device] > Security tab
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Dashboard shows 'Encryption: Compliant' or equivalent green status indicator. Red or 'Non-Compliant' requires immediate action.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Workspace ONE UEM, call the device search endpoint and inspect the 'DataProtection' and 'IsCompromised' fields along with the encryption-specific compliance attribute.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response includes 'ComplianceSummary' with an entry for the encryption policy rule showing 'Status': 'Compliant'.

option_description: Indicates whether the device user has configured a passcode or PIN. On iOS this is the primary prerequisite for activating hardware-backed data protection classes — without a passcode, iOS file encryption keys are derived without a user secret, rendering hardware encryption ineffective against offline attacks. On Android a passcode is typically required to enforce file-based encryption and unlock the credential-encrypted storage tier.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'unencrypted_device_storage' when 'input.mdm_compliance_encryption_status == "unknown"' AND 'not input.passcode_set'. This combination represents the worst-case uncertainty scenario: the MDM cannot confirm encryption state, and the known prerequisite (passcode) for iOS hardware encryption is absent. Even if the encryption flag is set, an iOS device without a passcode does not engage the protection class keys that prevent offline decryption, making this attribute a critical encryption dependency.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Jamf Pro MDM for the 'Passcode Present' field in the device security profile, which directly reflects whether the user has set a device passcode.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output prints 'True' confirming a passcode is set; 'False' indicates no passcode and requires immediate remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, open the device record and navigate to the Hardware section. Locate the 'Password' group and check 'Password required' compliance state. Additionally, check Device Compliance policies for the passcodeRequired rule result.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center: Devices > All Devices > [Device] > Hardware > Password section
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Field shows 'Password required: Yes' and the compliance policy evaluation for passcode is 'Compliant'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android via ADB, check whether a password has been set by inspecting the lock settings provider, which reflects current credential enrollment state.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell settings get secure lockscreen.password_type
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns a non-zero integer (e.g., 65536 for PIN, 196608 for alphanumeric password); returns 0 or null if no passcode is set.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If MDM enrollment is absent or the MDM reports unknown status, conduct a physical spot-check of devices by having users power the screen off and on, confirming a credential prompt appears before the home screen is accessible.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Device displays a lock screen requiring PIN, password, or biometric input after screen wake; no prompt indicates passcode is absent.

option_description: Reflects the patching completeness of the device operating system relative to all security updates published by the vendor. 'fully_patched' means all available security patches have been applied and the security patch level is current. 'partially_patched' means some but not all security updates are applied (common with carrier-delayed Android OEM updates). 'unpatched' means the device has not received any recent security updates despite their availability.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'outdated_os_version_with_unpatched_vulnerabilities' when 'input.os_patch_status in ["unpatched", "partially_patched"]'. Unpatched devices carry known public CVEs affecting the OS kernel, WebKit/Blink rendering engines, media frameworks, and Bluetooth stacks. These vulnerabilities enable sandbox escapes, privilege escalation to root, and zero-click exploitation via malicious network packets or media files. This is a high-criticality, score-8 finding categorized under network_security.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android: navigate to Settings > About Phone > Android Security Patch Level. Compare the displayed date against the current Google Android Security Bulletin (published monthly at source.android.com/security/bulletin). On iOS: navigate to Settings > General > About > iOS Version and compare against Apple's latest release at support.apple.com/en-us/111900.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Android: Settings > About Phone > Android Security Patch Level | iOS: Settings > General > About > iOS Version
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Android patch level matches the most recent monthly bulletin date (within 30–45 days). iOS version matches the latest release in Apple's support matrix.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android via ADB, retrieve the security patch level property and compare programmatically against the current expected patch date.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell getprop ro.build.version.security_patch && adb shell getprop ro.build.version.release
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ro.build.version.security_patch' returns a date string (e.g., '2024-11-01'); compare against current bulletin date to determine if fully_patched, partially_patched, or unpatched.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, query the managed device record for OS version and security patch level fields, then evaluate against Microsoft's compliance policy minimum OS version baseline.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON includes 'androidSecurityPatchLevel': '2024-11-01' (or equivalent iOS 'osVersion') and 'complianceState': 'compliant' confirming patches are current per MDM policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro, query the mobile device OS version and compare against the minimum OS version compliance criteria configured in the Smart Device Group or compliance policy.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns OS version string (e.g., '17.1.1'); cross-reference with Apple/Android vendor release notes to classify patch status.

option_description: Indicates whether the device is running an OS version that the vendor has officially discontinued security update support for. End-of-life status means the vendor will no longer publish security patches for any newly discovered vulnerabilities in that OS version, regardless of severity. This is distinct from patch status — an EOL device may be 'fully patched' for its last supported update but still permanently vulnerable to all subsequently disclosed CVEs.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'outdated_os_version_with_unpatched_vulnerabilities' unconditionally when 'input.os_end_of_life == true'. This is a standalone trigger independent of patch status because EOL devices cannot be remediated through patching — there are no patches available. An EOL iOS or Android version accumulates an ever-growing set of publicly known, unaddressed vulnerabilities including browser engine flaws, kernel privilege escalations, and Bluetooth stack issues that are trivially exploitable using public PoC code.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the device OS version from Settings > General > About (iOS) or Settings > About Phone > Software Information (Android), then cross-reference against the vendor EOL matrix: Apple publishes supported iOS versions implicitly via the release notes at support.apple.com; Android EOL varies by manufacturer — check the OEM's published support schedule (e.g., Samsung Software Update Policy, Google Pixel support page at support.google.com/pixelphone/answer/4457705).
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > General > About > iOS Version | Android: Settings > About Phone > Software Information > Android Version
how_to_obtain.expected_output: OS version is listed as currently supported on vendor's official support matrix page. Versions not listed as supported are EOL.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android via ADB, retrieve the SDK API level and cross-reference against Google's Android version distribution and OEM support schedules to determine EOL status.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell getprop ro.build.version.sdk && adb shell getprop ro.product.manufacturer && adb shell getprop ro.product.model
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SDK level (e.g., 28 = Android 9) compared against manufacturer support tables; SDK levels 28 and below are EOL for most OEMs as of 2024.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, query the compliance policy evaluation results for the 'minOSVersion' rule. Devices failing this rule are running versions below the organization-defined minimum, which should be set to reflect current supported versions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Compliance state for 'osMinimumVersion' rule shows 'compliant'; 'nonCompliant' indicates the device runs a version below minimum support threshold.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the MDM administrator to generate a fleet-wide report filtered by OS version and compare against the current vendor EOL schedule. For Apple devices, also verify against Apple's HT201222 security content page to confirm the last OS release date for the installed major version.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Fleet report shows no devices running iOS versions older than the current major release minus one (Apple typically supports N and N-1), or Android versions beyond OEM-published support windows.

option_description: Tracks the number of calendar days elapsed since the device last applied a security patch. On Android this maps to the Security Patch Level date visible under About Phone; on iOS it corresponds to the date of the last OS update installed.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'outdated_os_version_with_unpatched_vulnerabilities' exposure when this value is >= 90 days. Devices with stale patches carry publicly known kernel and framework CVEs that can be exploited for privilege escalation, sandbox escape, and malware installation. Even partially patched devices remain at risk for the unfixed subset of vulnerabilities.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android, navigate to Settings > About Phone > Android Security Patch Level. Note the displayed date and calculate elapsed days from today. On iOS, navigate to Settings > General > About and note the iOS Version, then cross-reference the release date from Apple's security release history at support.apple.com/en-us/111900.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Android: Settings > About Phone > Android Security Patch Level | iOS: Settings > General > About > Software Version
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A date string such as '2024-09-05' (Android) or a version like '17.6.1' with a known release date (iOS).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM platform API to retrieve the security patch date field for a specific device. For Microsoft Intune, call the Microsoft Graph API managed devices endpoint and inspect the 'androidSecurityPatchLevel' or 'osVersion' field, then compute delta to today.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing androidSecurityPatchLevel as a date string (e.g., '2024-09-01') for Android devices or an iOS version string for Apple devices.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jamf Pro environments, use the Jamf Pro API to retrieve the computer or mobile device record and extract the OS version or patch-level field, then compare to known release dates.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A version string such as '17.6.1' (iOS) which maps to a specific Apple Security Release date for elapsed-day calculation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If no MDM is present, instruct users to report their Security Patch Level or iOS version via a standardized self-attestation form. Cross-reference submitted versions against the vendor patch release calendar to compute days_since_last_security_patch.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A populated spreadsheet or ticketing system entry with device identifier, reported patch/OS version, and calculated days since last patch.

option_description: Boolean flag indicating whether the MDM platform, mobile threat defense (MTD) agent, or device attestation API has positively identified the device as jailbroken (iOS) or rooted (Android). A true value means OS security boundaries have been deliberately removed and elevated-privilege access is confirmed.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'device_jailbreak_or_root_status' on any true value for this attribute. A jailbroken or rooted device disables code-signing enforcement, app sandboxing, and Secure Enclave protections, exposing all application data, session tokens, and credentials to any process running at elevated privilege. The risk is compounded when mdm_compliance_status is 'unmanaged' or 'unknown'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM console API for the device's jailbreak/root detection status. In Microsoft Intune, retrieve the 'isJailBroken' property from the managed devices Graph API endpoint.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON field 'isJailBroken' returning 'True' or 'False'. A 'True' value maps to jailbreak_root_detected = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Jamf Pro admin console, navigate to Devices > Search Inventory, open the device record, and inspect the Security section for 'Jailbreak Detected' status. In VMware Workspace ONE (UEM), navigate to Devices > List View, open the device, and review the Security tab for compromise indicators.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro: Devices > Search Inventory > [Device] > Security | Workspace ONE UEM: Devices > List View > [Device] > Security
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A boolean or Yes/No field labeled 'Jailbreak Detected' or 'Compromised Device' set to No for compliant devices.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If a mobile threat defense (MTD) solution such as Lookout, Zimperium, or CrowdStrike Falcon for Mobile is deployed, query its API for the device threat assessment record and inspect the jailbreak/root detection flag.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Threat entries with type 'jailbreak' or 'root' and status 'active' confirm detection. No matching entries or status 'resolved' indicates clean state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the iOS DeviceCheck or Android Play Integrity API attestation results stored in the application backend. A failed or MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY=false response indicates device integrity compromise.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Play Integrity verdict JSON showing MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY=false or iOS DeviceCheck bit indicating a previously flagged device.

option_description: Boolean flag indicating whether the MTD agent or application runtime integrity check has observed artifacts consistent with sandbox escape — including presence of jailbreak binaries (Cydia, Magisk Manager), access to file system paths outside the application container, or active hooking frameworks (Substrate, Frida) injected into the process space.
security_impact: The Rego policy independently triggers 'device_jailbreak_or_root_status' on a true value here, separate from the MDM-reported jailbreak flag. This attribute catches evasion scenarios where the device passes MDM compliance checks but runtime evidence reveals active sandbox bypass. Frida or Substrate injection enables live memory inspection, credential extraction, and API interception of the running application.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MTD agent's local or cloud API for runtime threat events associated with the device. Filter for event types related to hooking framework detection, abnormal file path access, or known jailbreak binary presence.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of runtime events. Any entry with type 'hooking_framework_detected', 'jailbreak_binary_present', or 'sandbox_path_escape' sets this attribute to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the MTD console (e.g., Zimperium zConsole, Lookout MES, or CrowdStrike Falcon for Mobile), navigate to the device's threat history and review application-level runtime detections. Look for entries indicating Cydia, Magisk, Substrate, or Frida activity.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Zimperium zConsole: Devices > [Device] > Threat History > App Threats | Lookout MES: Devices > [Device] > Security Events
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Threat log showing no entries for hooking or bypass categories confirms false state. Any active detection entry confirms true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review application-side runtime integrity logs collected by an in-app RASP (Runtime Application Self-Protection) SDK or application shielding solution (e.g., Guardsquare DexGuard, Appdome). These SDKs log sandbox bypass attempts to the application's backend or a SIEM.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RASP event log entries tagged with 'FRIDA_DETECTED', 'HOOK_DETECTED', or 'JAILBREAK_ARTIFACT' for the target device identifier.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If MTD telemetry is forwarded to a SIEM (Splunk, Elastic), query for sandbox bypass indicators for the device in the last 30 days.
how_to_obtain.command: index=mtd_events device_id="<device_id>" (threat_type="hooking" OR threat_type="jailbreak_artifact" OR threat_type="sandbox_escape") | stats count by threat_type, timestamp
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero results confirm no observed bypass evidence. Any matching event rows confirm app_sandboxing_bypass_evidence = true.

option_description: The overall compliance verdict for this device as assessed and reported by the MDM/EMM platform. Reflects whether the device satisfies all MDM-enforced policies collectively (OS version, encryption, passcode, jailbreak status). Distinct from security_policy_compliance_state in that it also informs whether remediation of other findings (e.g., jailbreak) is enforceable.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this attribute in the 'device_jailbreak_or_root_status' rule: when mdm_compliance_status is 'unmanaged' or 'unknown' and jailbreak_root_detected is true, the risk is compounded because no policy enforcement mechanism exists to remediate the compromise. An 'unmanaged' or 'unknown' status signals the device is operating outside organizational control entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Microsoft Intune via Graph API to retrieve the complianceState field for the specific managed device, which maps directly to the enum values.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: complianceState field returning one of: 'compliant', 'noncompliant', 'unknown', 'notApplicable'. Map 'noncompliant' to non_compliant and absent devices to unmanaged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Jamf Pro admin console, navigate to Devices > Search Inventory, locate the device record, and review the Management Status and Compliance sections. In Workspace ONE UEM, navigate to Devices > List View and inspect the Compliance Status column.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro: Devices > Search Inventory > [Device] > General > Management Status | Workspace ONE UEM: Devices > List View > Compliance Status column
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A status indicator labeled 'Managed / Compliant', 'Non-Compliant', or 'Not Enrolled'. Unrecognized or absent device records map to unmanaged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jamf Pro, use the Classic API or Jamf Pro API to retrieve managed device status including management and compliance state.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: managed = 'true' with compliance_state = 'Compliant' maps to compliant. managed = 'false' maps to unmanaged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For devices not appearing in any MDM console, mark mdm_compliance_status as 'unmanaged'. Conduct a device inventory audit comparing the asset register against MDM enrollment records to identify unmanaged endpoints.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Devices present in the asset register but absent from MDM enrollment records are classified as unmanaged.

option_description: Captures the precise enrollment lifecycle state of the device within the MDM/EMM platform. Distinguishes between actively managed devices, inactive enrollments (lost MDM contact), pending onboarding, and entirely unenrolled devices. This consolidated flag drives multiple exposure rules because enrollment state determines the availability of remote wipe, certificate trust policy enforcement, and audit log forwarding.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this attribute across three rules: 'disabled_or_absent_mobile_device_management' fires when status is 'not_enrolled' or 'pending_enrollment'; 'absence_of_remote_wipe_capability' fires when status is 'enrolled_inactive' or 'not_enrolled' without remote wipe; and 'lack_of_certificate_pinning_enforcement_at_device_trust_store' and 'absence_of_device_level_audit_logging' also reference enrollment state. An inactive or absent enrollment means no security baseline is enforced and loss or theft cannot be remotely remediated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, navigate to Devices > All Devices, search by device name or serial number, and inspect the Management State and Enrollment Date columns. Inactive devices show a last check-in timestamp older than the MDM heartbeat threshold (typically > 30 days).
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune: Devices > All Devices > [Device] > Overview — Management State and Last Check-In fields
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Management State = 'Managed' with recent last check-in = enrolled_active. Management State = 'RetirePending' or stale check-in = enrolled_inactive. Device not found = not_enrolled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the device itself, verify MDM profile installation. On iOS: Settings > General > VPN & Device Management — the presence of a listed MDM profile confirms enrollment. On Android: locate the Device Policy or Intune Company Portal app and confirm it shows 'Active enrollment'.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > General > VPN & Device Management | Android: Device Policy app > Enrollment Status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: iOS: A named MDM configuration profile visible under VPN & Device Management. Android: Device Policy app showing enrolled organization account. Absence of either confirms not_enrolled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Intune Graph API to query enrollment state programmatically for a device identified by serial number.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices?$filter=serialNumber eq "<serial>"' | jq '.value[] | {id, managementState, enrolledDateTime, lastSyncDateTime}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: managementState = 'managed' with lastSyncDateTime within past 7 days = enrolled_active. managementState = 'retirePending' = enrolled_inactive. Empty value array = not_enrolled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For organizations without a unified MDM, cross-reference the device asset register against enrollment lists from all MDM platforms in use (Jamf, Intune, Workspace ONE). Devices appearing in the asset register but absent from all MDM consoles are classified as not_enrolled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A reconciled inventory showing enrollment status per device. Gap analysis identifies not_enrolled and pending_enrollment populations.

option_description: Unified boolean indicating whether a mechanism exists to remotely wipe or lock the device — combining MDM-initiated wipe/lock actions and platform-native find-my services (Apple Find My, Google Find My Device). True only when at least one operational remote wipe pathway is confirmed available and functional for the device.
security_impact: Two Rego rules reference this attribute. 'disabled_or_absent_mobile_device_management' fires when enrollment is inactive or absent AND remote wipe is not enabled. 'absence_of_remote_wipe_capability' fires independently when remote_wipe_capability_enabled is false regardless of enrollment status. Without this capability, lost or stolen devices permanently retain all application data, session tokens, and cached credentials with no organizational recovery path.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the MDM admin console, locate the device record and verify that wipe and lock actions are available and not grayed out. In Intune: Devices > All Devices > [Device] > select the device and confirm 'Wipe' and 'Remote Lock' actions appear in the action bar. In Jamf Pro: Devices > [Device] > Management Commands — verify 'Remote Wipe' is available.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune: Devices > All Devices > [Device] > action bar (Wipe, Remote Lock) | Jamf Pro: Devices > [Device] > Management Commands > Remote Wipe
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active, clickable Wipe and Remote Lock action buttons confirm MDM-based remote wipe capability = true. Grayed-out or absent actions indicate the MDM channel is not functional for this device.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify platform find-my service enrollment as a secondary wipe pathway. On iOS: Settings > [Apple ID] > Find My > Find My iPhone — confirm it is ON. On Android: Settings > Security > Find My Device — confirm it is enabled and the device appears in the Google Find My Device portal at android.com/find.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > [Apple ID] > Find My > Find My iPhone | Android: Settings > Security > Find My Device OR android.com/find
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Find My iPhone = On (iOS) or device listed in Google Find My Device portal with erase option available (Android) confirms platform-native wipe capability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Intune Graph API to confirm that remote wipe action is available for the device by checking its management state and action availability.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: managementState = 'managed' with no pending failed wipe actions confirms wipe capability is available. managementState = 'retirePending' or 'wipePending' with prior failure suggests degraded capability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the MDM administrator to confirm that automated wipe policies are configured (e.g., wipe on excessive failed passcode attempts, wipe on MDM non-compliance after grace period). Review MDM policy configurations to verify these automations are active and tested.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented MDM policy showing automatic wipe triggers and a recent test execution log confirming the wipe command was received by a test device.

option_description: The device's current compliance verdict against the organization's specific MDM-enforced security baseline policies, including encryption requirements, passcode complexity thresholds, and minimum OS version constraints. This is distinct from mdm_compliance_status in that it specifically reflects policy baseline adherence rather than overall MDM health.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this attribute in 'disabled_or_absent_mobile_device_management': when security_policy_compliance_state is 'non_compliant' or 'unknown' and the device is not actively enrolled, the exposure fires. A non_compliant state means the device is operating below the organization's minimum security baseline — such as running a prohibited OS version, missing encryption, or having an insufficient passcode — while potentially still being enrolled in MDM.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, navigate to Devices > Compliance Policies > select the applicable policy > Device Status. Filter for the specific device to see its individual policy compliance state. Alternatively, open the device record and navigate to Device Compliance to see per-policy results.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune: Devices > Compliance Policies > [Policy] > Device Status > filter by device name | OR Devices > All Devices > [Device] > Device Compliance
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A per-device compliance summary showing 'Compliant', 'Not Compliant', or 'Not Evaluated'. Per-setting breakdown shows which specific baseline settings are failing.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Intune Graph API for device compliance policy states to retrieve the security baseline compliance result for the target device.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array where state = 'compliant' for all entries maps to compliant. Any state = 'nonCompliant' entry maps to non_compliant. Empty array or device not found maps to unknown.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro, navigate to Computers or Mobile Devices, select the device, and review the Compliance section in the device record for policy compliance status. For mobile devices with Jamf Compliance Editor policies, check the Compliance Frameworks tab.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro: Devices > [Device Record] > Compliance | Jamf Pro: Devices > [Device] > Compliance Frameworks
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A compliance status indicator showing Pass/Fail against each enrolled security framework or policy set. Overall Fail state maps to non_compliant.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Workspace ONE UEM, use the REST API to retrieve the device's compliance policy evaluation results.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array of policy results. All ComplianceStatus = 'Compliant' maps to compliant. Any 'NonCompliant' entry maps to non_compliant. No MDM record maps to unknown.

option_description: Controls whether the device OS is configured to automatically join open (unauthenticated, unencrypted) Wi-Fi networks when they are in range, without prompting the user. On iOS this corresponds to the 'Ask to Join Networks' and 'Auto-Join Hotspot' settings; on Android it corresponds to 'Connect to open networks' or per-SSID auto-connect toggles.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'insecure_wi_fi_auto_connect_behavior' when auto_connect_open_networks_enabled is true AND vpn_always_on_enabled is false. Automatic connection to open networks allows an adversary to broadcast a known SSID and silently intercept all device traffic through a rogue access point, including application API calls, authentication headers, and session tokens, without any user awareness or interaction.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS: navigate to Settings > Wi-Fi and verify that 'Ask to Join Networks' is set to 'Ask' (not 'Notify' or 'Off', which allow automatic connection). Also check Settings > Wi-Fi > Auto-Join Hotspot is set to 'Never' or 'Ask to Join'. On Android (stock): Settings > Network & Internet > Wi-Fi > Wi-Fi Preferences > 'Connect to open networks' — confirm this toggle is OFF.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > Wi-Fi > Ask to Join Networks (set to 'Ask') | Android: Settings > Network & Internet > Wi-Fi > Wi-Fi Preferences > Connect to open networks
how_to_obtain.expected_output: iOS: 'Ask to Join Networks' = 'Ask' and 'Auto-Join Hotspot' = 'Never' or 'Ask' confirms auto-connect disabled. Android: 'Connect to open networks' toggle = OFF confirms disabled. Either platform showing auto-connect ON maps to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If MDM is deployed, query the MDM API to inspect the Wi-Fi configuration profile pushed to the device. For Intune, retrieve the device configuration profile assignments to check for a Wi-Fi payload that restricts open network auto-join.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>/deviceConfigurationStates' | jq '[.value[] | select(.displayName | test("Wi-Fi|Network"; "i")) | {profile: .displayName, state: .state}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration state entries for Wi-Fi profiles showing 'compliant' indicate a restricting Wi-Fi policy is applied. Absence of any Wi-Fi configuration profile suggests no MDM-enforced restriction on auto-connect behavior.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the MDM admin console, review the deployed Wi-Fi configuration profiles for the device's assigned groups. In Intune: Devices > Configuration Profiles — inspect Wi-Fi payload for 'Disable MAC address randomization', 'Auto Join', or equivalent open-network restriction settings. In Jamf Pro: Configuration Profiles > Wi-Fi Payload.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune: Devices > Configuration Profiles > [Wi-Fi Profile] > Properties | Jamf Pro: Configuration Profiles > [Profile] > Wi-Fi Payload
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A Wi-Fi configuration payload with 'Auto Join' = false and no open-network SSID entries confirms restriction is enforced. Absence of any Wi-Fi payload means device settings are user-controlled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the MDM administrator to confirm whether a Wi-Fi restriction policy explicitly prohibiting auto-connection to open networks has been deployed to all device groups. Review MDM policy documentation and change logs to verify this control is intentionally enforced rather than left to user discretion.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy documentation confirming a Wi-Fi payload with open-network auto-join disabled, applied to all enrolled device groups. Absence of such documentation suggests the setting is unmanaged and potentially enabled by default on end-user devices.

option_description: Controls whether the device automatically reconnects to any previously joined Wi-Fi SSID without prompting the user for confirmation. When enabled, the device will silently join any network broadcasting a known SSID, including adversary-controlled rogue access points.
security_impact: The Rego rule `insecure_wi_fi_auto_connect_behavior` fires when `auto_rejoin_known_networks_enabled == true` and `vpn_always_on_enabled` is absent or false. This combination allows an attacker to broadcast a spoofed SSID matching any network the device has previously joined, causing the device to silently associate and route all application traffic through the attacker's infrastructure. Without VPN as a compensating control, all unencrypted traffic and TLS sessions subject to interception are exposed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS, navigate to Settings > Wi-Fi, tap the (i) icon next to any saved network, and check whether the 'Auto-Join' toggle is enabled. Repeat for all saved networks. On Android, navigate to Settings > Network & Internet > Wi-Fi > Saved Networks, select each entry, and verify the 'Auto-reconnect' or 'Connect automatically' toggle state.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > Wi-Fi > [Network Name] > Auto-Join toggle | Android: Settings > Network & Internet > Wi-Fi > Saved Networks > [Network Name] > Auto-reconnect
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Toggle should be OFF for all saved networks; any network showing Auto-Join/Auto-reconnect ON is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM (e.g., Jamf Pro, Microsoft Intune, VMware Workspace ONE) for the Wi-Fi configuration payload deployed to the device. For iOS MDM payloads, retrieve the com.apple.wifi.managed profile and inspect the 'AutoJoin' key. For Android Enterprise, review the Wi-Fi network policy in the management console for auto-connect settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro: Devices > [Device] > Management > Configuration Profiles > Wi-Fi Payload > AutoJoin field | Intune: Devices > Configuration Profiles > Wi-Fi Profile > Connect automatically
how_to_obtain.expected_output: MDM payload should show AutoJoin=false or 'Connect automatically' disabled for all managed Wi-Fi profiles.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android devices with ADB access (for assessor/MDM-managed devices), use ADB shell to query Wi-Fi configuration. Note: this requires USB debugging to be enabled or an authorized MDM channel.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Review output for saved networks; cross-reference with device Wi-Fi settings to confirm auto-join state for each entry.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS managed devices, review the installed configuration profile XML (exportable from MDM or Apple Configurator 2) for Wi-Fi payloads. Locate the PayloadType com.apple.wifi.managed and inspect the AutoJoin boolean key.
how_to_obtain.file_path: /Library/ManagedPreferences/ (MDM-pushed profiles visible via Apple Configurator 2 or MDM export)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: <key>AutoJoin</key><false/> should be present for all Wi-Fi payload entries.

typical_values: true (default on most consumer OS configurations)

option_description: Controls whether the device enforces an always-on VPN configuration that tunnels all network traffic through a trusted VPN gateway at all times, regardless of the Wi-Fi network the device joins. This acts as a compensating control against rogue access point attacks by encrypting traffic before it traverses the untrusted local network.
security_impact: The Rego rule `insecure_wi_fi_auto_connect_behavior` uses `vpn_always_on_enabled` as a compensating control — if this is true, the auto-rejoin or auto-connect findings are suppressed even when auto-join is active. Without always-on VPN, any automatic Wi-Fi connection to a spoofed SSID exposes all device traffic. The absence of this control is evaluated alongside `auto_rejoin_known_networks_enabled` and `auto_connect_open_networks_enabled`, meaning the risk is compounded when both auto-connect and VPN absence are present simultaneously.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS unmanaged devices, navigate to Settings > VPN & Device Management > VPN and verify if a VPN profile is configured and whether it is set to connect automatically or always-on. On Android, navigate to Settings > Network & Internet > VPN, tap the gear icon next to any VPN entry, and check for 'Always-on VPN' toggle.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > VPN & Device Management > VPN | Android: Settings > Network & Internet > VPN > [Profile] > Always-on VPN
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Always-on VPN toggle should be enabled; if no VPN profile is configured, this is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the MDM-deployed VPN payload for the device. On iOS, query the MDM for com.apple.vpn.managed profile with 'OnDemandEnabled' set to true or an AlwaysOn VPN configuration (available on supervised iOS devices via com.apple.vpn.managed.applayer or per-app VPN). On Android Enterprise, check for lockdown VPN mode in the device policy.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro: Devices > [Device] > Management > Configuration Profiles > VPN Payload > OnDemandEnabled | Intune: Devices > Configuration Profiles > VPN Profile > Always-on VPN
how_to_obtain.expected_output: OnDemandEnabled=true (iOS) or lockdown VPN mode enabled (Android Enterprise) should be present in the deployed profile.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review organizational MDM policy documentation and network security architecture to confirm that an always-on VPN policy is formally defined, deployed to all mobile device fleet members running the dedicated application, and that VPN bypass exceptions are documented and justified.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy document confirming always-on VPN is enforced via MDM for all in-scope devices, with no unapproved exceptions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: While connected to a controlled test Wi-Fi network, capture traffic from the device using a network tap or managed wireless access point. Verify that all device traffic appears as VPN-encapsulated (e.g., IPsec ESP, WireGuard, or SSL VPN traffic to the corporate gateway) with no cleartext or non-VPN traffic visible.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All traffic from the device IP should appear as encrypted VPN tunnel traffic; any cleartext HTTP, DNS outside the tunnel, or direct internet traffic is a finding.

option_description: Indicates whether the dedicated application has been granted OS-level permissions that go beyond what its documented operational function requires. This is a qualitative assessment comparing the application's actual granted permissions against the permissions strictly necessary for its defined feature set.
security_impact: The Rego rule `excessive_application_permissions_granted` fires immediately when `app_permissions_exceed_requirements == true`, regardless of other factors. This is the most direct trigger for the exposure. Overly broad permissions expand the blast radius of any application compromise — a vulnerability in the app or a malicious SDK bundled within it gains access to microphone, camera, contacts, or storage that the application has no legitimate need for. This directly enables data exfiltration and surveillance without requiring privilege escalation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Android applications, decompile or inspect the APK's AndroidManifest.xml to enumerate all declared and requested permissions. Compare each permission against the application's documented feature set. Use tools such as apktool or aapt2 to extract the manifest without full decompilation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of uses-permission entries; each entry must map to a documented feature. Any permission without a justified feature is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For iOS applications, inspect the application's Info.plist for NSUsageDescription keys (e.g., NSMicrophoneUsageDescription, NSCameraUsageDescription, NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription, NSContactsUsageDescription). Cross-reference each declared permission with the application's functional requirements documentation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only permissions with corresponding operational justifications should be present; undocumented permissions are a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the device, navigate to the OS app permissions settings and review permissions granted to the specific application. On iOS: Settings > Privacy & Security > [Permission Category] > [App Name]. On Android: Settings > Apps > [App Name] > Permissions. Document all granted permissions and compare against the application's documented feature requirements.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > Privacy & Security > [each category] | Android: Settings > Apps > [App Name] > Permissions
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All granted permissions should correspond to documented features; any permission granted that has no feature justification is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the application's security and functional requirements documentation, design specifications, or data flow diagrams to determine the minimal permission set required. Compare documented required permissions against actually granted permissions. Interview the application development or product team if documentation is absent.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented requirements list should match or be a superset of the granted permissions; any permission granted beyond requirements is a positive finding.

typical_values: true (common in applications with legacy permission requests or third-party SDK requirements)
true (applications bundling advertising SDKs that request broad permissions)

option_description: An enumerated list of high-sensitivity OS permissions actually granted to the dedicated application or co-resident applications on the device. Captures the specific permission identifiers (e.g., RECORD_AUDIO, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, READ_CONTACTS) that have been granted at runtime or install time, providing concrete evidence of the device's permission exposure surface.
security_impact: The Rego rule `excessive_application_permissions_granted` fires when `count(sensitive_permissions_granted) > 0` and `permission_review_performed` is absent or false, and also when `co_resident_app_risk_level` is high or unknown with any sensitive permissions present. A non-empty list of sensitive permissions combined with lack of formal review or high-risk co-resident apps creates the exposure. Each permission in this list represents a specific data class (audio, precise location, contacts, files) that could be harvested by a compromised app or malicious SDK.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android devices with ADB access, enumerate all granted permissions for the target application package. Replace 'com.example.targetapp' with the actual package name.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell dumpsys package com.example.targetapp | grep -E 'permission|RECORD_AUDIO|CAMERA|READ_CONTACTS|ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION|READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE|WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output lists each permission with 'granted=true' or 'granted=false'; collect all sensitive permissions where granted=true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM management console for the device's application permission report. In Microsoft Intune, use the Graph API endpoint to retrieve managed app permissions. In Jamf Pro, use the Jamf Pro API to retrieve mobile device application inventory including permission grants.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro: Devices > [Device] > Inventory > Installed Apps > [App] > Permissions | Intune: Devices > [Device] > Discovered Apps
how_to_obtain.expected_output: MDM report listing all permissions granted to the managed application; export and filter for sensitive permission identifiers.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Manually enumerate sensitive permissions on-device for both the target application and all co-resident applications. On Android: Settings > Privacy > Permission Manager, then review each sensitive category (Microphone, Camera, Contacts, Location, Files & Media) for all apps with access. On iOS: Settings > Privacy & Security, then review each permission category.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Android: Settings > Privacy > Permission Manager > [each sensitive category] | iOS: Settings > Privacy & Security > [each sensitive category]
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Complete list of applications with access to each sensitive permission category; document all granted permissions for the target app and flagged co-resident apps.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For a comprehensive assessment, extract the permission grants from the Android permission database on a rooted/MDM-accessible device, or from the iOS privacy TCC database on a managed/supervised device where accessible via MDM tooling.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: XML containing granted runtime permissions per package; parse for sensitive permission identifiers and their granted state.

option_description: Indicates whether a formal, documented review of the application's requested and granted OS permissions has been completed against its operational requirements and approved by an appropriate authority. This is a process control confirming that permission grants are intentional and justified rather than default or incidental.
security_impact: The Rego rule `excessive_application_permissions_granted` fires when `count(sensitive_permissions_granted) > 0` and `permission_review_performed` is absent or false. The absence of a formal review means that even if sensitive permissions appear operationally justified, there is no documented assurance that they were deliberately scoped. This control acts as a gating condition — without it, any non-empty sensitive permissions list creates the exposure finding. It also validates that the permission scope was not inadvertently expanded by SDK updates or permission creep over application lifecycle.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request and review the application's security assessment records, change management tickets, or mobile application security testing (MAST) reports that specifically address permission scope. Verify that the review document enumerates each granted sensitive permission, maps it to a specific application feature, and carries an approver signature or ticket approval.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A dated document or ticket showing explicit permission-to-feature mapping, reviewer identity, and approval status for the current application version.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the application owner, mobile security team, or MDM administrator to determine whether a permission review process exists. Ask specifically whether reviews are triggered on new app versions, permission scope changes, or SDK updates, and request evidence of the most recent completed review.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Interviewee can produce a review document or reference a tracked process; inability to produce evidence is a finding regardless of claimed practice.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the organization's application security program tooling (e.g., a GRC platform, security ticketing system, or AppSec tracking tool) for a recorded permission review artifact linked to the mobile application's current production version.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GRC/AppSec portal: Application Registry > [App Name] > Security Reviews > Permission Scope Review
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Review record with status 'Completed/Approved', review date, reviewer, and current application version reference.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check MDM policy documentation or the application's deployment runbook for a permission baseline definition. A well-maintained MDM deployment should have a configuration baseline document listing approved permissions for the managed application.
how_to_obtain.file_path: MDM policy documentation / application deployment runbook (organizational document store)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Document listing approved permission set with justifications; absence of such documentation is a finding.

typical_values: false (most BYOD and unmanaged deployment contexts)
false (common even in MDM-managed environments without a mature AppSec program)
true (organizations with formal mobile application security review gates)

option_description: An assessed risk classification of other applications installed on the device alongside the dedicated application. Risk level is determined based on factors including MDM policy compliance status, whether apps were sourced from official or unofficial app stores, presence of known advertising or tracking SDKs, and mobile threat defense (MTD) tool findings.
security_impact: The Rego rule `excessive_application_permissions_granted` fires when `co_resident_app_risk_level in ['high', 'unknown']` and `count(sensitive_permissions_granted) > 0`. High or unknown co-resident app risk means that other applications on the device may share process space, access the same external storage, or leverage legitimately granted permissions to exfiltrate data that overlaps with the dedicated application's data scope. A high-risk co-resident app with storage or contacts access could harvest data written by the target application. 'Unknown' risk is treated as equivalent to 'high' in the policy, reflecting the principle that unassessed risk is not acceptable risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM console for a full application inventory for the target device and compare installed applications against the organization's approved application allowlist. Flag any applications not on the allowlist, from unknown sources, or flagged by the MDM compliance engine as policy violations.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune: Devices > [Device] > Discovered Apps (compare against Approved Apps list) | Jamf Pro: Devices > [Device] > Inventory > Installed Apps | Workspace ONE: Devices > [Device] > Apps
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of installed apps; apps outside the approved list or flagged as non-compliant indicate elevated co-resident app risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Integrate with a Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) solution (e.g., Lookout, Zimperium zIPS, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on mobile, Symantec Endpoint Security) and query the device's threat assessment report for co-resident application risk findings, SDK reputation flags, or malware detections.
how_to_obtain.navigation: MTD console: Devices > [Device] > Threat Assessment > Application Risk | Zimperium: Device Detail > App Analysis | Lookout: Device Profile > App Risk
how_to_obtain.expected_output: MTD report classifying co-resident app risk level; any 'high' or 'critical' app findings set the overall risk level to 'high'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android devices with ADB access, enumerate all installed user applications and cross-reference package names against known advertising/tracking SDK databases (e.g., Exodus Privacy database) to identify apps with known data-harvesting SDKs.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell pm list packages -3 | awk -F: '{print $2}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of third-party package names; cross-reference against Exodus Privacy (https://reports.exodus-privacy.eu.org) or similar SDK reputation database for tracker presence.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Manually review installed applications on the device through Settings. On iOS: Settings > General > iPhone Storage (lists all installed apps). On Android: Settings > Apps. Identify apps from unknown developers, sideloaded APKs (Android), or apps with disproportionate permission grants relative to their stated function.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > General > iPhone Storage | Android: Settings > Apps > See All Apps
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any unrecognized, sideloaded, or MDM-flagged applications present alongside the dedicated application; these raise the co-resident risk classification.

typical_values: unknown (default on unmanaged or newly assessed devices)
low (MDM-managed devices with enforced app allowlist)
medium (devices with unreviewed but store-sourced apps)
high (devices with sideloaded apps, MTD alerts, or known tracking SDK presence)

option_description: Indicates the current operational state of the device's Bluetooth radio. When Bluetooth is enabled persistently, the device maintains an active radio presence that can be detected and targeted by proximity-based attacks. This attribute captures whether Bluetooth is on at the time of assessment, serving as the prerequisite condition for Bluetooth-based attack surface evaluation.
security_impact: The Rego rule `bluetooth_perpetually_enabled_and_discoverable` requires both `bluetooth_enabled == true` and `bluetooth_discoverable_mode == true` with `bluetooth_policy_enforced` absent to trigger. Bluetooth enabled alone is not sufficient to trigger the finding, but it is a necessary condition. A perpetually enabled Bluetooth radio increases exposure to BlueBorne attack variants, Bluetooth impersonation attacks (BIAS), and KNOB attacks that exploit the baseband radio layer. On personal devices used for operational purposes, always-on Bluetooth without policy governance expands the proximity attack surface in public environments.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Directly inspect the device Bluetooth state. On iOS: Settings > Bluetooth — the toggle state indicates enabled/disabled. Note that the Control Center toggle does not fully disable Bluetooth on iOS 11+; only the Settings toggle provides a true disable. On Android: Settings > Connected Devices > Connection Preferences > Bluetooth or Settings > Bluetooth.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > Bluetooth (toggle state) | Android: Settings > Connected Devices > Bluetooth (toggle state)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Bluetooth toggle should be OFF when not in active use; any persistent ON state in an uncontrolled environment is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android devices with ADB access, query the current Bluetooth power state through the settings provider.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell settings get global bluetooth_on
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns '0' (disabled) or '1' (enabled). Value of '1' in a production context without compensating controls is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM management console for the device's Bluetooth state. Most MDM platforms report Bluetooth status as part of device inventory. In Jamf Pro, check device detail under Hardware; in Intune, check device hardware details in the Endpoint Manager portal.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro: Devices > [Device] > Hardware > Bluetooth Enabled | Intune: Devices > [Device] > Hardware
how_to_obtain.expected_output: bluetoothEnabled field showing 'false'; 'true' in a production device without Bluetooth policy enforcement is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the MDM policy configuration for a Bluetooth restriction payload. On iOS, a com.apple.applicationaccess restriction with 'allowBluetooth: false' would disable Bluetooth. On Android Enterprise, verify the bluetoothBlocked policy key in the device compliance/configuration profile.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro: Devices > Configuration Profiles > Restrictions Payload > Bluetooth | Intune: Device Configuration > Restrictions > Bluetooth
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Bluetooth restriction policy in place (allowBluetooth=false or bluetoothBlocked=true) for production devices; absence of a restriction policy indicates uncontrolled Bluetooth state.

typical_values: true (majority of personal devices; Bluetooth rarely disabled by users)
false (managed devices with MDM Bluetooth restriction policy)
true (devices where Bluetooth is enabled for legitimate use such as peripherals or health monitoring)

option_description: Indicates whether the device is actively broadcasting its presence to all nearby Bluetooth scanning devices, making it visible for uninvited pairing attempts and reconnaissance. Discoverable mode is distinct from Bluetooth being enabled — a device can have Bluetooth active for connected peripherals while not advertising itself to unknown devices.
security_impact: The Rego rule `bluetooth_perpetually_enabled_and_discoverable` fires when both `bluetooth_enabled == true` and `bluetooth_discoverable_mode == true` without `bluetooth_policy_enforced`. Discoverable mode is the critical escalating factor — without it, a Bluetooth-enabled device is less exposed since attackers must know the device's address. In discoverable mode, the device actively responds to inquiry scans, revealing its MAC address, device name, and supported Bluetooth profiles to any nearby scanner. This enables targeted BlueBorne exploitation, BIAS attacks that impersonate previously paired devices, and social engineering through visible device names. The Rego policy fires this rule twice on the same conditions, reinforcing that the combined state of enabled plus discoverable without policy control is the complete risk condition.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android devices with ADB access, query the Bluetooth adapter scan mode to determine if the device is in discoverable mode. SCAN_MODE_CONNECTABLE_DISCOVERABLE (3) indicates discoverable; SCAN_MODE_CONNECTABLE (2) indicates connectable but not discoverable; SCAN_MODE_NONE (0) indicates Bluetooth is off.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output containing 'SCAN_MODE_CONNECTABLE' only (not DISCOVERABLE) is acceptable; 'SCAN_MODE_CONNECTABLE_DISCOVERABLE' is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android, Bluetooth discoverability is typically time-limited and activated via Settings > Connected Devices > Pair New Device (which enables a temporary discoverable window). Persistent discoverability often requires developer options or third-party apps. Check Settings > Bluetooth to see if the device appears visible to nearby devices. On iOS, persistent discoverability for general Bluetooth (not specific profiles like AirDrop or BLE peripherals) is controlled by the OS and is generally not user-configurable; assess via MDM policy state.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Android: Settings > Connected Devices > Pair New Device (check if discoverable window is permanently active) | iOS: Assess via MDM profile or Settings > General > AirDrop (adjacent discoverability surface)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Device should not be in a persistent discoverable state; a permanent discoverable mode is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the MDM policy for Bluetooth governance controls. For iOS supervised devices, query the configuration profile for com.apple.applicationaccess restrictions on Bluetooth. For Android Enterprise, verify whether the Bluetooth discoverability is addressed in the device policy through the management console. Check whether bluetooth_policy_enforced (a compensating control referenced in the Rego policy) is confirmed through MDM documentation.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune: Endpoint Security > Device Configuration > [Policy] > Bluetooth settings | Jamf Pro: Configuration Profiles > Restrictions > Bluetooth Allow/Deny
how_to_obtain.expected_output: MDM policy explicitly restricting Bluetooth discoverability or blocking unpaired connections; absence of any Bluetooth governance policy is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Using a Bluetooth scanning tool on a separate device (e.g., a laptop with hcitool on Linux, or a dedicated Bluetooth scanner app), scan for nearby Bluetooth devices while in proximity to the target device. Verify whether the device appears in the scan results by its device name or MAC address.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Target device should NOT appear in the scan results; if the device name or MAC address appears in scan output, it is in discoverable mode and is a finding.

typical_values: false (default on iOS; iOS devices are not persistently discoverable for classic Bluetooth)
false (Android devices return to non-discoverable after the 2-minute pairing window expires)
true (Android devices with persistent discoverability enabled via developer options or third-party apps)

option_description: Controls whether an MDM or EMM policy profile is actively pushing and enforcing Bluetooth restrictions on the device — including disabling Bluetooth entirely or restricting the device from entering discoverable mode. Without this policy, Bluetooth state is left to user discretion.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'bluetooth_perpetually_enabled_and_discoverable' fires when bluetooth_enabled and bluetooth_discoverable_mode are both true and bluetooth_policy_enforced is absent or false. Without MDM enforcement, users can leave Bluetooth on and discoverable indefinitely, exposing the device to proximity attacks including BlueBorne variants and BIAS attacks that enable unauthorized pairing or traffic interception without any network access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune admin center, navigate to Devices > Configuration Profiles. Filter by platform (iOS/Android). Open the relevant device compliance or restrictions profile and confirm a Bluetooth restriction rule is present and assigned to the device group.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Devices > Configuration Profiles > [Profile Name] > Properties > Bluetooth settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Profile shows 'Block Bluetooth' or 'Restrict Bluetooth discoverable mode' set to Enabled, with status 'Succeeded' on the target device.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Microsoft Graph API to retrieve the device configuration profile applied to a specific device and check for Bluetooth restriction settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing a configuration state entry referencing a Bluetooth restriction profile with settingStates showing 'compliant'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro, navigate to Computers/Mobile Devices > Policies or Configuration Profiles. Open the assigned profile for the device and inspect the Restrictions payload for Bluetooth controls.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro > Mobile Devices > Configuration Profiles > [Profile] > Restrictions > Bluetooth
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Restriction payload shows 'Allow Bluetooth to be toggled off' unchecked or 'Force Bluetooth Always On' not set, indicating active Bluetooth governance.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android via Android Debug Bridge (ADB), check the global Bluetooth setting state to infer whether MDM policy has locked it down.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell settings get global bluetooth_on && adb shell dumpsys bluetooth_manager | grep -i 'enabled\|state\|discoverable'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows Bluetooth state; cross-reference with MDM console to confirm the state is policy-enforced rather than user-set.

option_description: Controls whether the device operating system permits application installation from sources outside the official platform store (Google Play or Apple App Store). On Android this maps to the 'Install Unknown Apps' or legacy 'Unknown Sources' toggle. On iOS it corresponds to the presence of enterprise or developer provisioning profiles that allow distribution of unsigned or third-party-distributed IPAs.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'unmanaged_sideloaded_or_third_party_store_applications' fires directly when unknown_sources_installation_enabled is true. Sideloaded applications bypass platform-level malware scanning (Google Play Protect, App Store review), enabling credential-harvesting, surveillance functionality, or compromised SDKs to be installed and persist on devices that also run the monitored application.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android, manually navigate device settings to check the Unknown Sources toggle state.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Android: Settings > Security > Install Unknown Apps — review each listed app to see if 'Allow from this source' is enabled for any.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All listed apps show 'Not allowed' under Install Unknown Apps. If any show 'Allowed', the control is non-compliant.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use ADB to query the secure settings value for installation of unknown applications on Android.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell settings get secure install_non_market_apps && adb shell pm list packages -i | grep -v 'com.android\|com.google'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: install_non_market_apps returns '0' (disabled). Package list shows only store-sourced apps (installer indicated as com.android.vending or null).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Intune Graph API for the Android compliance policy setting that covers unknown sources installation on enrolled devices.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: settingState shows 'compliant' for SecurityBlockUntrustedApps, indicating unknown sources is blocked by policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS, check for unauthorized enterprise or developer provisioning profiles that enable sideloading.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > General > VPN & Device Management — review all listed profiles. Any profile from an unrecognized enterprise or developer account indicates potential sideloading capability.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only MDM enrollment profile from the known organizational MDM vendor is present. No third-party enterprise distribution certificates are listed.

option_description: Controls whether the MDM solution is actively pushing and enforcing an application allowlist or blocklist policy on the device. When enforced, only approved applications from authorized sources can be installed or run; attempts to run blocked or unlisted applications are prevented by MDM policy rather than user discretion.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'unmanaged_sideloaded_or_third_party_store_applications' has a second trigger: it fires when mdm_app_allowlist_enforced is absent or false, regardless of whether unknown sources is explicitly enabled. This means even if the sideloading toggle appears off, absence of an active MDM allowlist leaves the app ecosystem uncontrolled, allowing malicious or unauthorized applications to persist without detection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, verify that a Managed App Configuration or App Protection Policy with application restrictions is applied and compliant on the target device.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Apps > App Protection Policies > [Policy Name] > Properties > Apps list; then check Devices > [Device] > App Configuration Policies for applied status.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: App protection or configuration policy shows 'Succeeded' installation status on the device with a defined allowlist of approved app bundle IDs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Jamf Pro API to retrieve managed app configuration profiles for a specific mobile device and confirm allowlist enforcement.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response lists managed applications with enforcement state. If the list is empty or enforcement is set to 'optional', the allowlist is not active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In SOTI MobiControl, navigate to the device profile and review App Management rules to confirm a blocklist or allowlist policy is assigned.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SOTI MobiControl > Profiles > [Device Profile] > App Management > App Rules — check for presence of Allowed Apps or Blocked Apps lists with enforcement status.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: App Management rule shows a populated allowlist or blocklist with enforcement mode set to 'Mandatory' or 'Enforced', not 'Optional'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the MDM administrator to confirm whether app allowlist policies are actively assigned to the device group containing production mobile devices, and whether compliance reporting validates enforcement.
