how_to_obtain.expected_output: Administrator can demonstrate a named MDM policy profile containing app restrictions assigned to the production device group with documented compliance reporting cadence.

option_description: Controls whether the mobile application itself implements certificate pinning — validating that TLS connections are made only to servers presenting certificates matching a pre-configured public key hash or certificate hash, independent of the device's trust store. This makes the application immune to trust store manipulation or rogue CA attacks.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'lack_of_certificate_pinning_enforcement_at_device_trust_store' fires when certificate_pinning_enforced is absent/false, combined with user-installed CAs present or network security config not restricting user CAs. Without pinning, any CA trusted by the device can sign a fraudulent certificate for the application's backend, enabling transparent MITM interception of all application traffic including authentication tokens and session data.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android, decompile the APK and inspect the OkHttp or Retrofit client configuration for CertificatePinner usage, or check for TrustKit initialization in the Application class.
how_to_obtain.command: apktool d application.apk -o decompiled/ && grep -r 'CertificatePinner\|TrustKit\|pinCertificate\|sha256\|PublicKeyPin' decompiled/smali/ decompiled/res/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Grep results show CertificatePinner.Builder with .add() entries containing sha256/ pin hashes, or TrustKit.initializeWithNetworkSecurityConfiguration() call.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android, check the Network Security Config XML for certificate pinning configuration alongside trust anchor restrictions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: XML contains <pin-set> element with <pin digest='SHA-256'>...</pin> entries scoped to the application's backend domain.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to intercept application traffic using a proxy (Burp Suite) with a custom CA installed on the device. If pinning is enforced, the application will fail to connect and may display a certificate error.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Application fails with SSL handshake error or connection refused when routed through the intercepting proxy, confirming pinning is active. Successful interception indicates pinning is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS, inspect the application's Info.plist for NSAppTransportSecurity settings and search the binary for TrustKit or AFNetworking pinning configuration.
how_to_obtain.command: plutil -p Payload/Application.app/Info.plist | grep -A 10 'NSAppTransportSecurity' && strings Payload/Application.app/Application | grep -i 'pinnedkey\|sha256\|sslpin'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Binary strings include SHA-256 pin hashes or Info.plist references to pinning configuration. Absence of these strings suggests no pinning is implemented.

typical_values: false (majority of consumer and enterprise apps)

option_description: Indicates whether the device's operating system trust store contains one or more CA certificates that were manually installed by the device user — as opposed to certificates distributed by the OS vendor or pushed through MDM policy. User-installed CAs are trusted by all applications that rely on the system trust store for TLS validation.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'lack_of_certificate_pinning_enforcement_at_device_trust_store' fires when certificate_pinning_enforced is false AND user_installed_ca_certificates_present is true. A user-installed CA can be attacker-controlled (e.g., installed as part of a phishing campaign or malware) and used to issue valid-looking certificates for any domain, enabling MITM of all application TLS traffic without triggering certificate validation errors in apps that rely solely on the device trust store.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android, navigate to the User credentials section within Security settings to enumerate user-installed CA certificates.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Android: Settings > Security > Encryption & Credentials > Trusted Credentials > User tab — any entries listed here are user-installed CAs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: User tab is empty, indicating no user-installed CA certificates are present. Any listed entries represent a risk requiring investigation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android via ADB, list CA certificates in the user certificate store directory to detect user-installed CAs.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell ls -la /data/misc/user/0/cacerts-added/ 2>/dev/null || adb shell ls -la /data/data/com.android.providers.settings/databases/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Directory is empty or does not exist, indicating no user-installed CAs. Files present in this directory represent user-added CA certificates.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS, navigate to Certificate Trust Settings to check for user-installed CA certificates that have been granted full trust.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings — certificates listed here have been manually trusted by the user beyond standard iOS trust.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No certificates appear under Certificate Trust Settings. Any listed certificate requires investigation to determine if it is organizational or potentially malicious.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM console for device certificate inventory to remotely identify user-installed CA certificates without physical device access.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: MDM certificate inventory report shows only OS-vendor and MDM-issued certificates. User-installed CAs would appear as unmanaged certificates not matching known MDM-distributed certificates.

typical_values: true (common in testing environments, corporate MITM proxies, or compromised devices)

option_description: Controls whether the application has implemented an explicit network security configuration that prevents it from trusting user-installed CA certificates, even if those CAs are present in the device trust store. On Android this is achieved via the Network Security Config XML manifest; on iOS it is governed by App Transport Security (ATS) settings and NSURLSession configuration.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'lack_of_certificate_pinning_enforcement_at_device_trust_store' fires when both certificate_pinning_enforced is false AND network_security_config_restricts_user_cas is false. This attribute is the secondary defense: even without full certificate pinning, an application that explicitly excludes user CAs from its trust anchors cannot be intercepted via a user-installed rogue CA. Without this control and without pinning, any user-installed CA on the device can be used to perform transparent MITM of all application traffic.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android, decompile the APK and inspect the Network Security Config XML for trust-anchors that explicitly exclude user-installed CAs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: XML contains <trust-anchors><certificates src='system'/></trust-anchors> without any <certificates src='user'/> element, confirming user CAs are excluded. Presence of src='user' or absence of explicit trust-anchors indicates non-compliant configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android, verify the AndroidManifest.xml references the network security config and that cleartextTrafficPermitted is false.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AndroidManifest.xml contains android:networkSecurityConfig='@xml/network_security_config' and cleartextTrafficPermitted='false' or it is absent (defaulting to false on API 28+).

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS, inspect the application's Info.plist for NSAppTransportSecurity settings that govern CA trust behavior and cleartext permissions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NSAllowsArbitraryLoads is absent or false, NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsInWebContent is absent or false, and no NSExceptionDomains with NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads entries exist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Install a self-signed or proxy CA certificate into the device user trust store, then route application traffic through a MITM proxy. If the application rejects connections when the proxy CA is user-installed (but not system-installed), network security config is correctly restricting user CAs.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout proxy-ca.key -out proxy-ca.crt -days 365 -nodes && mitmproxy --certs *=proxy-ca.crt --listen-port 8080
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Application fails TLS handshake when proxy CA is user-installed only, confirming the app excludes user trust anchors. If interception succeeds, the control is absent.

typical_values: false (default on Android API < 24 or when no explicit NSC is defined)
true (properly hardened applications with explicit NSC or ATS configuration)

option_description: Indicates the current state of the device-level cloud backup service — specifically whether iCloud Backup (iOS) or Google One/Drive Backup (Android) is enabled at the OS level. When enabled, the platform periodically transmits device data including installed application data containers to cloud infrastructure controlled by the platform vendor, outside organizational boundaries.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'icloud_or_cloud_backup_containing_application_data' fires when platform_cloud_backup_enabled is true AND application_data_excluded_from_backup is false AND mdm_backup_restriction_enforced is also absent. Platform backups can capture application data containers including session tokens, cached credentials, and offline configuration files. This data is then stored in cloud accounts potentially secured only by the user's personal platform credentials, creating an exfiltration surface entirely outside the organization's control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS, check the iCloud Backup status directly on the device.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > [Your Name / Apple ID] > iCloud > iCloud Backup — check whether 'Back Up This iPhone' toggle is ON or OFF. Note the 'Last Backup' timestamp if enabled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Toggle is OFF, indicating iCloud Backup is disabled. Toggle ON with a recent 'Last Backup' timestamp confirms backup is actively occurring.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android, check Google backup status in system settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Android: Settings > System > Backup — check 'Back up to Google Drive' toggle status and review 'Backup by Google One' or equivalent section.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Backup toggle is OFF. If ON, the timestamp of the last backup and included data categories confirm what is being backed up.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Intune Graph API to check the device's backup compliance state or applied restriction profiles targeting backup services.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>' | jq '{complianceState, managementState, isEncrypted, deviceEnrollmentType}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Device record should be cross-referenced with an applied configuration profile that sets 'Block iCloud backup' or equivalent. Absence of such a profile indicates backup may be user-controlled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android via ADB, check the backup transport configuration to determine if cloud backup is active.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell bmgr enabled && adb shell bmgr list transports
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Backup Manager currently enabled: true' with active transport set to 'com.google.android.gms/.backup.BackupTransportService' confirms Google backup is active. 'false' indicates backup is disabled.

typical_values: true (default on both iOS and Android for personal accounts)

option_description: Controls whether the monitored application has explicitly declared its data container — including stored tokens, cached credentials, offline configuration, and session state — as excluded from platform cloud backup operations. On iOS this is implemented via NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey on sensitive file paths. On Android it is implemented via android:allowBackup=false in the manifest or a backup rules XML that enumerates paths to exclude.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'icloud_or_cloud_backup_containing_application_data' fires when platform_cloud_backup_enabled is true and application_data_excluded_from_backup is false (and mdm_backup_restriction_enforced is also absent). Even if device-level backup cannot be MDM-restricted (common in BYOD scenarios), an application that explicitly excludes its own data container from backup prevents session tokens, API keys, and cached credentials from being replicated to the user's personal cloud account, significantly reducing the exfiltration surface.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android, inspect the AndroidManifest.xml for the allowBackup attribute and locate any referenced backup rules XML file.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: android:allowBackup='false' is the most restrictive setting. If allowBackup='true', a fullBackupContent or dataExtractionRules attribute should reference an XML file explicitly excluding credential and token storage paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android, if a backup rules XML is referenced, inspect it to confirm sensitive paths are excluded.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: XML contains <exclude domain='sharedpref' path='tokens.xml'/>, <exclude domain='database' path='session.db'/>, or equivalent entries covering all credential and token storage locations. Absence of exclusion entries for sensitive paths indicates a gap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS, decompile or inspect the IPA to check whether sensitive files are programmatically excluded from backup using NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Search returns source or compiled references to NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey set to true on the application's token storage directory (e.g., Application Support or Documents subdirectory containing credentials). No results indicate backup exclusion is not implemented.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a test iOS device, use iMazing or iTunes to perform a local backup and inspect the backup archive to verify whether application data from the monitored app is present.
how_to_obtain.command: idevicebackup2 backup --full /tmp/device_backup/ && find /tmp/device_backup/ -name 'Manifest.db' -exec sqlite3 {} 'SELECT relativePath, flags FROM Files WHERE relativePath LIKE "%<AppBundleID>%";' \;
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Query returns no rows or returns rows with flags value of 4 (indicating excluded) for sensitive application data paths. Rows with flags=1 (regular files) confirm the data is being backed up.

typical_values: false (default — most applications do not explicitly configure backup exclusions)
true (security-conscious applications with explicit manifest or code-level backup exclusions)

option_description: Controls whether an active MDM configuration profile enforces a policy that either fully disables cloud backup (e.g., iCloud on iOS, Google backup on Android) or specifically excludes the target application's data container from any backup operation on enrolled devices.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags 'icloud_or_cloud_backup_containing_application_data' when platform_cloud_backup_enabled is true, application_data_excluded_from_backup is absent, AND mdm_backup_restriction_enforced is false. Without this control, application tokens, cached credentials, and configuration data are replicated to cloud infrastructure outside organizational control, expanding the data exfiltration surface beyond the device perimeter.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Intune Graph API for iOS device configuration profiles and inspect the allowCloudBackup restriction key.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output showing 'iCloudBlockBackup: true' for the profile applied to production devices indicates restriction is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro, navigate to Computers/Devices > Configuration Profiles, open the relevant profile, and inspect the Restrictions payload for 'Allow iCloud Backup' checkbox state. For Android, review the Managed Configurations or Restrictions payload for backup policy.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro > Devices > Configuration Profiles > [Profile Name] > Restrictions payload > Functionality > Allow iCloud Backup
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Checkbox unchecked (disabled) confirms allowCloudBackup=false is enforced in the deployed profile.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query VMware Workspace ONE UEM REST API to retrieve device-assigned profiles and check backup restriction policy status.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Profiles with 'Active' status should include a profile containing backup restriction settings; cross-reference profile contents for backup block keys.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On an enrolled iOS device, navigate to Settings > General > VPN & Device Management, open the MDM profile, and review installed restrictions. Use Apple Configurator 2 to read a backup of the profile XML and grep for allowCloudBackup.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS Settings > General > VPN & Device Management > [MDM Profile] > More Details > Restrictions
how_to_obtain.expected_output: <key>allowCloudBackup</key><false/> present in the mobileconfig XML confirms the restriction is deployed.

typical_values: true (backup restriction actively enforced via MDM policy)

option_description: Indicates whether Android USB debugging (ADB — Android Debug Bridge) is currently active on the device. When enabled, any USB-connected host with adb installed can execute arbitrary shell commands, install or extract APKs, pull application data directories, and bypass some screen lock protections depending on OS version.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'developer_mode_or_usb_debugging_enabled' when usb_debugging_enabled is true AND device_environment is 'production' or 'unknown'. Enabling ADB on a production device provides an unauthenticated local attack surface: a physically adjacent attacker or malicious charging station can extract app data, install malware APKs, or execute commands within the application's sandbox without requiring device unlock on certain Android versions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If ADB access is already available (for authorized assessment), query the global ADB enabled setting directly on the device.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell settings get global adb_enabled
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns '1' if USB debugging is enabled; '0' if disabled. A result of 'null' typically means disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Directly on the Android device, navigate to Settings > System > Developer Options and check the USB Debugging toggle. Developer Options may be hidden; if so, the absence of the menu itself indicates developer mode is not activated.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Android Settings > System > Developer Options > USB Debugging toggle
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Toggle in OFF position confirms USB debugging is disabled. If the Developer Options menu does not appear, developer mode is inactive.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Intune Graph API for Android device compliance or configuration state, filtering for developer options policy enforcement.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices?$filter=operatingSystem eq %27Android%27' | jq '.value[] | {deviceName, complianceState, isSupervised}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cross-reference compliance state with an Android policy that includes 'androidDeviceOwnerGeneralDeviceConfiguration' restricting developer options. Non-compliant devices may have ADB enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro for Android or VMware Workspace ONE, navigate to the device record and review the Device Details or Security tab for 'Developer Mode' or 'ADB Enabled' property reported by the MDM agent.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Workspace ONE UEM Console > Devices > List View > [Device] > Security > Device Compromised Status / Developer Mode
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Field 'Developer Mode: Disabled' or 'ADB: Off' in device security details confirms the control is inactive.

typical_values: false (default on production devices — ADB disabled)
true (misconfiguration on production; expected only on development/test devices)

option_description: Indicates whether iOS Developer Mode (introduced in iOS 16) is currently enabled on the device. Developer Mode is a per-device toggle that must be explicitly activated and permits sideloading of unsigned or ad-hoc signed applications, attachment of debuggers, and use of device inspection tools such as Instruments or the iOS Simulator bridge — capabilities that are blocked on standard user devices.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'developer_mode_or_usb_debugging_enabled' when developer_mode_enabled is true AND device_environment is 'production' or 'unknown'. On a production device, enabled Developer Mode allows an attacker with brief physical access to sideload malicious applications, attach debuggers to running processes (including the target application), and use Xcode device instruments to inspect memory and file system contents — bypassing the protections enforced on non-developer devices.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the iOS device directly, navigate to Settings > Privacy & Security and check for the presence and state of the 'Developer Mode' toggle (visible only on iOS 16+). If the toggle is absent, Developer Mode has never been activated.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS Settings > Privacy & Security > Developer Mode (toggle)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Toggle showing 'Off' or toggle absent entirely confirms Developer Mode is disabled. Toggle 'On' with a confirmation badge indicates active developer mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM server (Intune or Jamf) for device properties that surface Developer Mode state. Jamf Pro reports this via the device inventory attribute under the mobile device detail endpoint.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON field 'developer_mode_enabled: false' confirms the control is inactive on the queried device.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Using Apple Configurator 2 or cfgutil on macOS, retrieve device state from a connected iOS device to check Developer Mode status.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output 'developerModeEnabled = 0' confirms Developer Mode is off. Requires Apple Configurator 2 and device connection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro, navigate to Devices > Mobile Devices > [Device Name] > General tab and review the 'Developer Mode Enabled' field in device inventory. For Intune, check the Device Details blade under Hardware properties.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro > Devices > Mobile Devices > [Device] > General > Developer Mode Enabled
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Field value 'No' or 'false' confirms developer mode is not active on the enrolled device.

typical_values: false (default; expected on all production iOS devices)
true (expected only on enrolled developer devices; misconfiguration in production context)

option_description: Classifies whether a device is a production end-user device, a development device used for application building and debugging, a test device used in QA/staging pipelines, or an unknown/unclassified device. This classification gates the interpretation of developer mode and USB debugging findings — these controls are intentionally enabled on development and test devices but represent genuine misconfigurations on production devices.
security_impact: The Rego policy evaluates 'developer_mode_or_usb_debugging_enabled' only when device_environment is 'production' or 'unknown'. Misclassifying a production device as 'development' would suppress a valid high-criticality finding, while an 'unknown' classification triggers the same exposure flag as production, enforcing a fail-secure default. Accurate environment classification is critical to preventing false negative suppression in the developer mode and USB debugging exposure checks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM device inventory for enrollment group, device category, or custom attribute that encodes environment classification. In Intune, device category corresponds directly to environment labels if configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: deviceCategoryDisplayName returns 'Production', 'Development', or 'Test' if device categories are configured in Intune; managedDeviceOwnerType distinguishes corporate vs. personal.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro, check the device's assigned Site, Department, or custom Extension Attribute that records deployment environment. Navigate to Devices > Mobile Devices > [Device] > General and review Department or Extension Attributes fields.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro > Devices > Mobile Devices > [Device] > General > Department / Extension Attributes
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Department field or Extension Attribute named 'Device Environment' returns 'Production', 'Development', 'Test', or similar label aligned to classification schema.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organization's device asset inventory or CMDB (ServiceNow, Lansweeper, or equivalent) to confirm environment classification for the device serial number or MDM device ID. Cross-reference naming conventions documented in device provisioning runbooks.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Asset record confirms device environment classification matches MDM group assignment; naming convention (e.g., 'DEV-', 'PROD-' prefix) provides secondary confirmation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query a custom device attribute or tag from the MDM API to retrieve environment classification programmatically for bulk assessment.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns string value such as 'production', 'development', 'test', or 'unknown' from the configured Jamf Extension Attribute.

typical_values: unknown (unenrolled or newly provisioned devices not yet classified)

option_description: Controls whether the device enforces an automatic lockout or data wipe action after a configured number of consecutive failed passcode or PIN entry attempts. When enabled, this policy prevents sustained brute-force attacks against short numeric PINs by triggering device lockout or erasure after the threshold is reached.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'insufficient_failed_authentication_lockout_policy' when failed_passcode_lockout_enabled is false (absent or explicitly disabled) OR when max_failed_attempts_threshold is 0. Without this control, an attacker with physical possession of a device can systematically attempt all combinations of a 4-digit PIN (10,000 combinations) without triggering protective erasure, particularly on devices without Secure Enclave throttling. This is rated low criticality in isolation but compounds physical access risks significantly.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS, navigate to Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions, or check Settings > Face ID & Passcode for 'Erase Data' toggle which wipes after 10 failed attempts. On Android, check Settings > Security > Screen lock settings for automatic wipe or lockout configuration.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iOS: Settings > Face ID & Passcode > Erase Data (toggle) | Android: Settings > Security > Screen Lock > Failed attempts
how_to_obtain.expected_output: iOS 'Erase Data' toggle enabled confirms wipe-after-10-attempts is active. Android confirmation dialog shows the configured failed attempt threshold before wipe or lockout.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the Intune device configuration profile for iOS and inspect the 'maximumPasscodeAttemptCount' key, or for Android inspect 'passwordSignInFailureCountBeforeFactoryReset'.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/deviceConfigurations' | jq '.value[] | select(."@odata.type" == "#microsoft.graph.iosGeneralDeviceConfiguration") | {displayName, maximumPasscodeAttemptCount, passcodeRequired}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: maximumPasscodeAttemptCount set to a value between 1–10 confirms lockout policy is configured. Null or absent value indicates lockout is not enforced via this profile.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Jamf Pro API for the device passcode policy configuration to retrieve max failed attempts setting.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cross-reference with configuration profile payload: PasscodePolicy > maxFailedAttempts should return a non-zero integer for lockout to be active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro, navigate to Configuration Profiles > [Profile] > Passcode payload and review the 'Maximum Number of Failed Attempts' field. In Intune, navigate to Devices > Configuration Profiles > [Profile] > Properties > Configuration Settings > Password.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune > Devices > Configuration Profiles > [Profile] > Properties > Configuration Settings > Password > Number of sign-in failures before wiping device
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Field populated with a value of 1–10 confirms failed passcode lockout is configured. Empty or '0' indicates the policy is absent.

typical_values: false (default — common on unmanaged or loosely managed devices)
true (enforced on MDM-managed corporate devices with passcode policies)

option_description: Specifies the exact integer value representing the maximum number of consecutive failed passcode or PIN attempts permitted before the device automatically triggers a lockout or wipe action. A value of 0 means no cap is configured (equivalent to failed_passcode_lockout_enabled being false). Values above 10 are considered weak by industry standards as they allow significant brute-force opportunity.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'insufficient_failed_authentication_lockout_policy' when max_failed_attempts_threshold is 0 (no limit) OR when failed_passcode_lockout_enabled is true but max_failed_attempts_threshold exceeds 10. A threshold above 10 on a 4-digit PIN allows over 10% of the full PIN keyspace to be attempted before erasure, making offline brute-force feasible for patient attackers with physical access. Value of 0 means unlimited attempts, entirely removing the protection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Intune Graph API for iOS passcode configuration profiles and extract the maximumPasscodeAttemptCount value from the relevant deployed profile.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array with maxAttempts field; values of 4–10 are compliant, null or 0 indicates no threshold configured, values >10 indicate weak policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Android Enterprise enrolled devices in Intune, retrieve the passwordSignInFailureCountBeforeFactoryReset value from the Android device restriction profile.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: passwordSignInFailureCountBeforeFactoryReset returns integer 1–10 for compliant configuration. Null indicates the wipe-on-failure policy is not set.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro, open the Mobile Device Configuration Profile, navigate to the Passcode payload, and read the 'Maximum Number of Failed Attempts' field value. In Workspace ONE, navigate to Profiles > [Profile] > Passcode > Max Failed Attempts.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro > Devices > Configuration Profiles > [Profile] > Passcode > Maximum Number of Failed Attempts
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer value displayed; acceptable range is 1–10. Value of 0 or blank indicates no cap is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On an enrolled iOS device with MDM profile exported, parse the mobileconfig XML for the maxFailedAttempts key value.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: <key>maxFailedAttempts</key><integer>6</integer> is an example of a compliant value. Integer greater than 10 or absent key indicates insufficient policy.

typical_values: 0 (default — no limit enforced, common on unmanaged devices)
11–20 (weak policy, technically configured but ineffective against brute force)

option_description: Indicates whether the device or its MDM management profile is configured to forward security-relevant events — such as failed authentication attempts, application installations, permission grants, and policy violations — to a centralized logging platform or SIEM system. This enables organizational visibility into endpoint security events beyond what is retained locally on the device.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'absence_of_device_level_audit_logging' when central_log_forwarding_enabled is false (among other conditions). Without centralized log forwarding, security incidents on the mobile endpoint — including credential theft attempts, unauthorized app installations, or policy tampering — cannot be detected in real time, correlated with other signals, or used for forensic reconstruction. This is a low-criticality finding in isolation but critically undermines incident response capability across the distributed mobile fleet.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the MDM console (Intune, Jamf, or Workspace ONE), navigate to the device's assigned configuration profiles and check for a logging or telemetry policy payload. In Intune, review Diagnostic settings and the Endpoint Analytics enrollment status.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune > Devices > [Device] > Device Configuration > Assigned Profiles > review for logging/telemetry profile | Endpoint Analytics > Device scores
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of an active logging or EDR agent profile (e.g., Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Splunk MINT, or custom syslog profile) with 'Succeeded' deployment status confirms forwarding is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Intune for devices enrolled in Endpoint Analytics or with a Microsoft Defender for Endpoint onboarding profile, which serves as a proxy for log forwarding capability.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: configurationManagerClientEnabledFeatures showing endpointProtection or inventory features enabled indicates telemetry forwarding is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the MDM/security operations team to confirm whether a SIEM integration (e.g., Splunk, Sentinel, Sumo Logic) ingests mobile device logs from the MDM platform's event stream or from an installed EDR agent on managed devices.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that MDM audit logs or device telemetry events are actively ingested by the SIEM, with evidence of a log source or connector configured for mobile device events.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the SIEM or logging platform for presence of mobile device event sources. Query Splunk or Sentinel for mobile-origin log events to confirm forwarding is operational.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Results containing device identifiers and security event types confirm active log forwarding from mobile devices to the central platform.

typical_values: false (default — most organizations do not configure mobile-to-SIEM log forwarding)
true (mature MDM deployments with Defender for Endpoint or dedicated EDR agents on managed devices)

option_description: Specifies the number of days that security-relevant audit events are retained locally on the device's storage before being overwritten or purged by the OS or logging framework. A value of 0 indicates that no local log retention is configured, meaning events are either not captured or are immediately discarded after the logging buffer cycles.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'absence_of_device_level_audit_logging' when local_audit_log_retention_days is 0 (no retention configured). Even when central log forwarding is not available (e.g., device offline, SIEM outage), local retention ensures that security events remain available for forensic investigation during incident response. Zero-day retention means any compromise, unauthorized access attempt, or data exfiltration occurring while the device is offline leaves no recoverable trace on the endpoint itself.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro or Workspace ONE, navigate to the device's assigned configuration profiles and look for a logging policy payload specifying retention duration. For iOS, review any custom Configuration Profile containing logging server or local storage settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Workspace ONE UEM > Devices > Profiles > [Device Profile] > Logging payload > Log Retention Period
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Retention period field displaying a value greater than 0 days (recommend minimum 30 days) confirms local log retention is configured. Absent field or value 0 indicates no retention policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM API for the logging configuration profile assigned to the device and parse retention settings from the profile payload.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u '<user>:<pass>' -H 'Accept: application/json' 'https://<jamf-host>/JSSResource/mobiledeviceconfigurations/id/<profile_id>' | jq '.configuration_profile.payloads | fromjson | .. | objects | select(.PayloadType=="com.apple.logging") | .LogRetentionDays'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer value for LogRetentionDays returned from the logging payload; 0 or absent indicates no local retention is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On an Android device (with adb access for authorized assessment), check the system log buffer size and ring buffer retention, which approximates local audit log retention capability.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell logcat -g && adb shell getprop persist.log.tag && adb shell settings get global event_log_size
how_to_obtain.expected_output: logcat -g returns ring buffer sizes (e.g., 'main: 256Kb, system: 256Kb'); absence of persistent log storage configuration indicates 0-day effective retention after reboot.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the MDM administrator or security operations team to determine whether a documented log retention policy exists for mobile devices, including whether any MDM-enforced or application-level logging agent is configured with a specific retention window.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation or MDM policy showing a retention value ≥30 days for local audit events, or confirmation that central forwarding compensates for absent local retention (which should still be reflected in central_log_forwarding_enabled).

typical_values: 0 (default — no configured local retention; most mobile deployments lack explicit log retention policy)
30 (common compliance minimum where local logging is configured)
90 (enterprise-grade retention aligned to incident response SLAs)

option_description: Controls which security-relevant event categories are actively captured on the device or forwarded to a centralized logging platform. Categories may include failed_auth, app_install, permission_grant, and device_unlock. An empty array means no device-level telemetry is being collected.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags absence_of_device_level_audit_logging when count(input.audit_event_types_captured) == 0, treating an empty set as a complete logging gap. Without captured event types, failed authentication attempts, unauthorized app installs, and permission escalations cannot be detected or attributed. This directly prevents incident reconstruction and defeats any detection capability for credential theft or malware persistence at the endpoint layer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, navigate to Devices > Monitor > Device compliance, select the target device, and inspect the 'Diagnostic data' and 'Managed app' logs section to see which event categories are configured for collection under the assigned compliance policy.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Devices > Monitor > Device compliance > [device] > Device diagnostics
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of event categories such as 'ComplianceLog', 'AppManagement', 'DeviceEnrollment' indicating what is being captured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Microsoft Graph API for the device's diagnostic configuration to enumerate instrumented event types. Replace {deviceId} with the Intune-assigned device object ID.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of compliance policy state names reflecting which event domains are monitored; empty array indicates no audit coverage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query your SIEM (e.g., Splunk or Microsoft Sentinel) for events tagged with the device's MDM-enrolled hostname or device ID to confirm which event categories are actually arriving. A search returning zero results confirms audit_event_types_captured is effectively empty.
how_to_obtain.command: index=mobile_devices sourcetype=mdm_events device_id="<device_id>" | stats count by event_category
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Table of event_category values with non-zero counts. Missing categories such as 'failed_auth' or 'app_install' represent gaps in capture configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the MDM administrator or review the MDM configuration profile XML/JSON deployed to the device to identify which logging or telemetry modules are enabled in the Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) or logging agent policy.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration profile should list PayloadType entries for logging agents (e.g., com.lookout.enterprise, com.zimperium.zips) with explicit event category parameters defined.
